T1.summary: T1 remained dominated by persistence of unresolved or invalid process states. X2-T1 broadened into SRE participation after repair but still exhausted the turn budget without repository consequence.

T2.summary: T2 was the most heterogeneous family. One file-target repair sharply redirected the suffix, two process/file interventions produced mixed continuations, and X4-T2 regenerated work from an already-finalized natural arm into a longer multi-role implementation path.

T3.summary: T3 ranged from clean historical-path suppression/redirection to route-only redirection and persistence, showing that removing or reopening a local legacy-path structure does not guarantee downstream closure across system conditions.

strongest_mechanism_observation.statement: The natural arm finalized after recognizing that a working payment flow already existed and made no repository change. The one-shot file-list process revision instead reactivated a 64-turn multi-role path and produced new app.js, checkout_app/api.py and index.html state, including a new /api/pay path. A local structural repair can therefore preserve its repair boundary while regenerating broader downstream work.

interpretation: G3 again separates repair locality from downstream efficacy: all 12 one-shot interventions preserved the repair boundary, while only three produced clean targeted suppression or redirection.
Four pairs remained persistent and four showed mixed downstream effects, so precise local mutation did not imply deterministic process closure.
X4-T2 is a particularly informative regeneration case because the natural suffix had already finalized while the repaired suffix reopened and expanded implementation work.
The T1 family shows that unresolved or invalid-envelope process states can remain inertial after a single local revision.
The result supports one-shot, fail-closed intervention accounting rather than automatic retry or outcome-forcing.
